text:
6.13 Troubleshooting

ValueError: reference and target must share the same shape

Align the images first (Chapter 5).

ValueError: kernel_shape must use odd dimensions

Use odd sizes, such as (19, 19).

ValueError: variance must be strictly positive

The variance holds zeros or negative values. Set those pixels to np.nan to leave them out of the fit.

ValueError: fit normal equations are ill-conditioned for the requested basis

Two basis components are the same or nearly so, or the fit pixels hold too little structure to tell the basis terms apart, such as blank sky. Drop a component, lower a degree, or fit pixels that include stars.

ValueError: fit region is underdetermined for the requested basis

The fit mask selects fewer pixels than the fit has coefficients. Select more pixels.

converged is False after solve_spatial_als

Raise max_iterations in SpatialALSConfig (--als-iterations on the command line), or set flux_conserve=True. SpatialALSConfig defaults to flux_conserve=False.

flux_conserve behaves differently in solve_separable_kernel

There it divides the kernel by its sum, which forces the sum to one. In the other solvers it rewrites the basis and the sum stays a fitted value.

ERROR: mask FITS is ambiguous; specify a mask HDU explicitly

The image file has no HDU named MASK. Pass the mask file, or the HDU index with --reference-mask-hdu or --target-mask-hdu.

ERROR: [Errno 17] File exists

The run directory exists already. Pass a new --name, or remove the old run.

A GPU fit reports backend cpu

auto falls back to the CPU when no GPU backend is usable. Check fit.backend, or pass backend="cupy" to raise an error instead.

title: 6  Subtract two images

text:
7.1 Make a difference image
xFit measures what a difference image holds at each candidate. Its nonlinear source and dipole fits use a batched Levenberg-Marquardt least-squares solver; fixed-position photometry uses a direct linear solution. A dipole is a positive and a negative lobe side by side. A source that moved between the two images leaves one, and so does a slightly misaligned star.
You need: cuPhoton installed with the CPU profile (Chapter 1), and a difference image with its variance and candidate positions (Chapter 6). This page makes them from a sample pair.
The two blocks run the alignment and subtraction of Chapter 6 in short form, without the refit.
import numpy as np
from astropy.wcs import WCS
from cuphoton.core.fits_io import read_fits_images
from cuphoton.xrep import BBox, ReprojectionSpec, make_wcs_pair_transform, reproject_masked_array

target_read, reference_read = (read_fits_images(f"sample/{name}.fits", [0]) for name in ("target", "reference"))
target, reference = (r.arrays[0].astype(np.float64) for r in (target_read, reference_read))
target_header, reference_header = target_read.infos[0].header, reference_read.infos[0].header
target_variance = np.clip(target, 0, None) / target_header["GAIN"]
reference_variance = np.clip(reference, 0, None) / reference_header["GAIN"]
spec = ReprojectionSpec(mapping=make_wcs_pair_transform(WCS(target_header), WCS(reference_header)),
                        output_bbox=BBox(0, 0, target.shape[1], target.shape[0]))  # (x, y) origin, then the size
aligned = reproject_masked_array(reference, reference_variance, np.zeros(reference.shape, dtype=bool), spec, backend="cpu")
from cuphoton.xpois import (GaussianBasisComponent, identify_residual_hotspots, solve_constant_kernel,
                            standardize_constant_kernel_residual)

basis = [GaussianBasisComponent(0.7, 4), GaussianBasisComponent(1.4, 2), GaussianBasisComponent(2.8, 2)]
fit = solve_constant_kernel(aligned.image, target, basis, kernel_shape=(19, 19),
                            variance=target_variance, background_degree=1, backend="cpu")
noise = standardize_constant_kernel_residual(fit.residual, kernel=fit.kernel, target_variance=target_variance,
                                             reference_variance=aligned.variance)
regions = identify_residual_hotspots(noise.standardized_residual, robust_sigma=1.0, max_regions=None)
difference, difference_variance = fit.residual, noise.marginal_residual_variance
print([region["peak_yx"] for region in regions])  # (y, x)

[[21, 72], [167, 80]]
The two candidates are the brightened star and the new source, at (y, x) pixels.
title: 7  Measure candidates

text:
7.2 Cut cutouts around the candidates
xFit takes cutouts as an array of shape (batch, y, x). window_stamps from xPois cuts a square window around each (x, y) position, with NaN outside the image. Cut the difference and its variance the same way.

from cuphoton.xpois import window_stamps

positions = np.array([region["peak_yx"][::-1] for region in regions], dtype=float)  # (x, y)
cutouts = window_stamps(difference, positions, 31)
cutout_variance = window_stamps(difference_variance, positions, 31)
usable = np.isfinite(cutouts) & np.isfinite(cutout_variance) & (cutout_variance > 0)
print(cutouts.shape, usable.sum(axis=(1, 2)), "usable pixels")

(2, 31, 31) [868 961] usable pixels


The first cutout reaches into the edge band and has fewer usable pixels. Inside a cutout, xFit positions are (x, y) pixels from the center pixel, which is (0, 0). The cutouts are 31 pixels wide to leave room for the quality flags’ optional noise calibration (Section 7.9); the flags themselves also work on smaller cutouts.

xFit has four ways to measure a cutout:









Call

title: 7  Measure candidates

text:
7.4 Fit one source per cutout
fit_single_sources fits one Gaussian lobe per cutout, from the start position you pass. With psf_sigma the lobe is round with that width, and only its amplitude and position are fitted. Without it, the widths and orientation are free. sign=+1 starts a brightening source and sign=-1 a fading one; without sign, a matched filter at the start sets it. This initializes the amplitude, whose fitted sign is free to change.

from cuphoton.xfit import fit_single_sources

psf_sigma = target_header["PSFSIG"]  # the target PSF width, in pixels
start = np.zeros((len(positions), 2))  # (x, y) offsets from each cutout center, all zero
sources = fit_single_sources(cutouts, cutout_variance, start, psf_sigma, mask=usable, sign=1)
for i in range(len(sources.x)):
    print(f"x {sources.x[i]:+.2f} +- {sources.position_error_x[i]:.2f}, y {sources.y[i]:+.2f} +- "
          f"{sources.position_error_y[i]:.2f}, flux {sources.flux[i]:.0f} +- {sources.flux_error[i]:.0f}, "
          f"converged {sources.converged[i]}")

x +0.46 +- 0.02, y -0.02 +- 0.02, flux 12234 +- 114, converged True
x +0.20 +- 0.04, y +0.05 +- 0.04, flux 4140 +- 71, converged True


flux is the nonnegative lobe-flux magnitude, \(2\pi|A|\sigma_x\sigma_y\) for fitted amplitude \(A\). Recover a signed difference flux with np.sign(sources.parameters[:, 0]) * sources.flux; sources.sign records the starting sign. The result also holds parameters, covariance, standard_errors, chi_square, uncertainty_valid and residuals (model minus data). Its covariance is a local, first-order estimate assuming independent pixels and the supplied variances. It does not account for a wrong PSF or pixel correlations.
title: 7  Measure candidates

section: 7.5 Measure the flux at a fixed position
text:
7.5 Measure the flux at a fixed position
forced_psf_photometry fits only the flux of a unit-flux Gaussian PSF at fixed positions. The model is linear in the flux. The flux and its error therefore follow without iteration. Pass the fitted positions, or positions from a catalog.

from cuphoton.xfit import forced_psf_photometry

fixed = np.column_stack([sources.x, sources.y])  # (x, y) from each cutout center
photometry = forced_psf_photometry(cutouts, cutout_variance, fixed, psf_sigma, mask=usable)
print("flux", photometry.flux.round(0), "error", photometry.flux_error.round(0), "valid", photometry.valid)

flux [12234.  4140.] error [114.  71.] valid [ True  True]


Here flux is signed: a fading source gives a negative value. flux_error assumes that the position and the PSF are right and the pixel noise is independent. It leaves out the uncertainty of a position fitted on the same image. To replace the Gaussian, pass unit-flux PSF cutouts, already evaluated at the positions, as psf=; the function does not normalize them. cuphoton.xpois.forced_flux_at applies this estimator to a full image at (x, y) positions. Set local_sky=False to match this example: its default subtracts each window’s median, without adding the uncertainty of that sky estimate to the flux error.
title: 7  Measure candidates

text:
7.6 Build a dipole cutout
The sample pair has no dipole. Build one with NumPy. A star of flux 6,000 sits at (x, y) = (2, 1) in the target and at (-1, -1) in the reference. The difference is target minus matched reference. The star therefore leaves a positive lobe where it is in the target and a negative lobe where it was in the reference. The noise matches the sky of the difference image.

rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
y, x = np.mgrid[-15:16, -15:16]  # pixels from the cutout center


def star(x0, y0, flux):
    return flux / (2 * np.pi * psf_sigma**2) * np.exp(-((x - x0) ** 2 + (y - y0) ** 2) / (2 * psf_sigma**2))


dipole_variance = np.full((31, 31), np.nanmedian(difference_variance))
dipole = star(2, 1, 6000) - star(-1, -1, 6000) + rng.normal(0, np.sqrt(dipole_variance))

text:
7.7 Fit dipoles
GaussianDipoleModel draws one elliptical Gaussian twice, with opposite signs. Both lobes share one amplitude, their peak height, and one shape, set by the widths sigma_x and sigma_y and the orientation theta. The other four parameters are the lobe centers x_pos, y_pos, x_neg and y_neg. The lobe at (x_pos, y_pos) has the sign of amplitude, and the lobe at (x_neg, y_neg) has the opposite sign. GaussianDipoleModel((31, 31)) takes the cutout shape, (height, width), which must match the images. model="gaussian" builds the same model from the image shape. Fit the two candidates and the dipole in one batch, with a mask that excludes every non-finite pixel.

from cuphoton.xfit import GaussianDipoleModel, fit_dipoles

images = np.concatenate([cutouts, dipole[None]])
variance = np.concatenate([cutout_variance, dipole_variance[None]])
mask = np.isfinite(images) & np.isfinite(variance) & (variance > 0)
dipoles = fit_dipoles(images, model=GaussianDipoleModel((31, 31)), variance=variance, mask=mask, backend="numpy")
print(dipoles.status, dipoles.uncertainty_valid, dipoles.uncertainty_reason)
for name, value, error in zip(dipoles.parameter_names, dipoles.parameters[2], dipoles.standard_errors[2]):
    print(f"{name:9s} {value:8.2f} +- {error:.2f}")

7.8 Derive catalog quantities
derived_dipole_quantities turns each Gaussian dipole fit into its center, the position of the positive lobe (where the source is in the target), the lobe separation and the lobe flux. It propagates the full covariance to each error. The cross terms matter, because amplitude and widths are anticorrelated.

from cuphoton.xfit import derived_dipole_quantities

q = derived_dipole_quantities(dipoles)
i = 2  # the dipole cutout
print(f"center (x, y) ({q.center_x[i]:+.2f}, {q.center_y[i]:+.2f}) +- ({q.center_x_error[i]:.2f}, {q.center_y_error[i]:.2f}) px")
print(f"separation {q.separation[i]:.2f} +- {q.separation_error[i]:.2f} px")
print(f"lobe flux {q.lobe_flux[i]:.0f} +- {q.lobe_flux_error[i]:.0f}")

7.9 Screen the fits with quality flags
A converged fit can still be wrong. dipole_quality_flags returns one integer of DipoleQualityFlag bits per fit. Set width_range from the PSF, for example 0.5 to 2.5 times its width.

from cuphoton.xfit import DipoleQualityFlag, dipole_quality_flags

flags = dipole_quality_flags(dipoles, images, variance=variance, mask=mask,
                             width_range=(0.5 * psf_sigma, 2.5 * psf_sigma))
for i, value in enumerate(flags):
    print(i, int(value), [flag.name for flag in DipoleQualityFlag if value & flag])

0 36 ['LOBE_OUTSIDE_STAMP', 'NEGATIVE_LOBE_UNSUPPORTED']
1 101 ['UNCERTAINTY_INVALID', 'LOBE_OUTSIDE_STAMP', 'NEGATIVE_LOBE_UNSUPPORTED', 'POSITIVE_LOBE_UNSUPPORTED']
2 0 []


Both candidates set NEGATIVE_LOBE_UNSUPPORTED and LOBE_OUTSIDE_STAMP. They are brightening single sources, with the spare lobe placed outside the cutout. Measure them with fit_single_sources. The new source’s spare lobe ran too far out for the lobe test, which then sets both NEGATIVE_LOBE_UNSUPPORTED and POSITIVE_LOBE_UNSUPPORTED. The dipole sets no flag. Read the bits together:








Bit
Flag
Set when




1
UNCERTAINTY_INVALID
the fit has no valid covariance


2
WIDTH_OUT_OF_RANGE
a fitted width lies outside width_range


4
LOBE_OUTSIDE_STAMP
a lobe center lies outside the cutout


8
NO_LOBE_AT_CANDIDATE
no lobe lies within center_radius pixels of the cutout center


16
LOBES_OVERLAP
the lobes are closer than overlap_separation pixels


32
NEGATIVE_LOBE_UNSUPPORTED
the lobes do not overlap and the negative lobe fails the lobe_snr significance test


64
POSITIVE_LOBE_UNSUPPORTED
the lobes do not overlap and the positive lobe fails the lobe_snr significance test



Test one bit with (flags & int(DipoleQualityFlag.LOBES_OVERLAP)) != 0. Exactly one unsupported-lobe bit suggests a brightening or fading single source; read it with the other flags, since a failed fit or unusable lobe can also set it. Closely overlapping lobes make amplitude and separation trade against each other. With calibrate_noise=True, the default, the flags can reduce lobe significance using its robust spread at empty positions of the cutout. This estimates the effect of correlated noise on the lobe test, not on the fitted covariance. Calibration needs at least 12 usable empty positions; even a large cutout can have too few.

7.11 Use a sampled PSF
StampDipoleModel shifts copies of a PSF image instead of drawing Gaussians. Its five parameters are the two lobe centers and one shared flux. Use it when you have an image of the PSF, such as a survey’s PSF model, and the PSF is not Gaussian. The block uses a sampled Gaussian as the PSF image.

from cuphoton.xfit import StampDipoleModel

py, px = np.mgrid[-7:8, -7:8]
psf = np.exp(-(px**2 + py**2) / (2 * psf_sigma**2))
stamp_model = StampDipoleModel(psf / psf.sum(), image_shape=(31, 31))
stamp_fit = fit_dipoles(dipole[None], model=stamp_model, variance=dipole_variance[None], backend="numpy")
print(dict(zip(stamp_fit.parameter_names, stamp_fit.parameters[0].round(2))))

7.13 On a GPU
With the gpu profile, pass backend="cupy" to fit_dipoles, which still returns NumPy arrays. fit_dipoles_device keeps the result on the GPU. The other xFit calls return CuPy arrays for CuPy inputs. The cutile and native backends fit Gaussian models only, as the xFit reference describes. cutile needs the cutile extra, and native needs the native extension (Chapter 1).

import cupy as cp

flags = dipole_quality_flags(on_device, d_images, variance=d_variance, mask=d_mask)  # CuPy flags

text:
7.15 Troubleshooting

ValueError: images must be finite on included pixels

Pass mask=np.isfinite(images) & np.isfinite(variance) & (variance > 0) so invalid image and variance pixels are both excluded.

UserWarning: 21x21 stamps hold fewer than 12 calibration positions

The optional noise calibration needs at least 12 usable empty positions. Square cutouts of 26 pixels or less cannot provide them. Cut larger cutouts, or pass calibrate_noise=False and interpret the lobe tests without a correlation correction.

uncertainty_valid is False

Read uncertainty_reason. A rank-deficient Jacobian means the data do not constrain a parameter, such as a spare lobe on a single source. Check the quality flags.

status is max_evaluations

The fit used up its evaluation budget before it converged. A slowly converging fit can need many evaluations under the default "v0.2" rules. converged is then False and the uncertainties are invalid. Raise max_evaluations in LMConfig, or pass --max-evaluations. A larger budget takes longer and does not guarantee convergence.

ValueError: derived quantities require a Gaussian dipole fit

derived_dipole_quantities and dipole_quality_flags take GaussianDipoleModel fits only.

ValueError: fusion requires backend='cupy' or 'cutile'

Fusion runs on cupy or cutile, with the Gaussian model only.

ERROR: output directory already exists

fit-dipoles needs a new --output-dir for every run.

text:
8.1 Make labeled cutouts
A real/bogus classifier scores cutouts around a candidate to distinguish the labeled real-source class from artifacts, such as cosmic rays or badly subtracted stars. xScan (cuphoton.xscan) trains and runs the transformer family of Inada et al. (2026) with PyTorch. Pair models use target and reference cutouts; triplet models also use the difference image. Its command-line workflow packages cutouts as a dataset, checks it, trains, evaluates, predicts and queues candidates for human review. Use xScan after Chapter 6 has found the candidates.
The output named probability is a sigmoid score between zero and one. Training does not calibrate it into an observed probability that a candidate is astrophysical. Check calibration and the operating threshold on representative held-out data before interpreting a score such as 0.9 as a 90% chance of being real.
You need:
The block below makes 240 synthetic candidates of 21 by 21 pixels, in units of the sky noise. Half are labeled real, with a new source in the target. The other half simulate artifacts: a stationary star misregistered by one pixel between the images, or a cosmic ray (one bright pixel in the target). A genuinely moving source can produce the same dipole shape; its label depends on your science target, not on the shape alone.
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n, size = 240, 21
yy, xx = np.mgrid[:size, :size] - size // 2


def psf(dx):  # a Gaussian point source, shifted dx pixels to the right
    return np.exp(-(yy**2 + (xx - dx) ** 2) / (2 * 1.5**2))


labels = np.tile([1, 0], n // 2)                          # 1 real, 0 bogus
kind = np.where(labels == 1, 0, rng.integers(1, 3, n))    # 0 new source, 1 misregistered star, 2 cosmic ray
peak = rng.uniform(5, 25, n)[:, None, None]
reference = rng.normal(0, 1, (n, size, size)).astype(np.float32)
target = rng.normal(0, 1, (n, size, size)).astype(np.float32)
target += np.where(kind[:, None, None] == 0, peak * psf(0), 0)
reference += np.where(kind[:, None, None] == 1, peak * psf(0), 0)
target += np.where(kind[:, None, None] == 1, peak * psf(1), 0)
target[kind == 2, size // 2, size // 2] += peak[kind == 2, 0, 0]
difference = target - reference
print(target.shape, target.dtype, "real:", labels.sum(), "bogus:", n - labels.sum())

(240, 21, 21) float32 real: 120 bogus: 120
Training and prediction use the cutouts as stored. They do not align, subtract or rescale them. Prepare every cutout the same way.

8.4 Train a model
Training reads a YAML file. The model settings below make a tiny network that trains in seconds on a CPU. For the default network, which takes 51-pixel cutouts, start from the repository’s examples/xscan/train-triplet.example.yaml.

import shutil

Path("runs").mkdir(exist_ok=True)
Path("runs/classify-train.yaml").write_text("""\
dataset_dir: sample/cutouts
output_root: runs
run_name: classify-demo
epochs: 2
batch_size: 16
early_stopping_metric: val_loss   # keep the epoch with the lowest validation loss
device: auto                      # CUDA when PyTorch finds a GPU, otherwise the CPU
model:
  image_size: 21                  # cutout side in pixels
  depths: [1, 1]                  # two small encoder stages, for this demo only
  num_heads: [1, 1]
  embed_dims: [16, 16]
  decoder_embedding_dim: 16
""")
shutil.rmtree("runs/classify-demo", ignore_errors=True)  # xScan never writes into an existing run

cuphoton xscan train-inada-triplet --config runs/classify-train.yaml > runs/classify-train.json
The run directory runs/classify-demo/ holds checkpoint.pt, the full configuration config.yaml, the per-epoch history.json and the run summary.json.

summary = json.loads(Path("runs/classify-train.json").read_text())
print("device:", summary["device"], "| saved epoch:", summary["early_stopping"]["best_epoch"],
      "| selected by:", summary["best_metric"]["name"])
for epoch in json.loads(Path("runs/classify-demo/history.json").read_text()):
    print(f"epoch {epoch['epoch']:.0f}: train loss {epoch['train_loss']:.3f}, "
          f"validation loss {epoch['val_loss']:.3f}, validation ROC AUC {epoch['val_roc_auc']:.3f}")

The checkpoint holds the epoch with the best selection metric, which is not always the last epoch. When early_stopping_metric is unset, selection uses validation ROC AUC (defined in the next step), or validation loss for a single-class validation split. Early stopping remains disabled unless a metric or patience is set.

8.5 Evaluate on the test split
evaluate-real-bogus scores one split, test by default, and writes metrics, curves and per-candidate predictions to runs/classify-demo/evaluation/test/.
cuphoton xscan evaluate-real-bogus --run-dir runs/classify-demo --dataset-dir sample/cutouts > runs/classify-evaluate.json

evaluation = json.loads(Path("runs/classify-evaluate.json").read_text())
print(f"ROC AUC {evaluation['roc_auc']:.3f}, PR AUC {evaluation['pr_auc']:.3f}")
thresholds = evaluation["threshold_diagnostics"]
for name, result in [("fixed", thresholds["fixed_threshold"]),
                     ("validation-selected", thresholds["validation_selected"]["evaluated_split_metrics"])]:
    print(f"{name} threshold {result['threshold']:.3f}: accuracy {result['accuracy']:.3f}, "
          f"real missed {result['fn']}, bogus passed {result['fp']}")

ROC AUC 1.000, PR AUC 1.000
fixed threshold 0.500: accuracy 0.950, real missed 2, bogus passed 0
validation-selected threshold 0.500: accuracy 0.950, real missed 2, bogus passed 0


ROC AUC measures how often a random labeled-real candidate outranks a labeled-bogus one, counting ties as half. PR AUC is the trapezoidal area under the precision-recall curve. A candidate is classified as real when its score reaches the threshold. Next to the fixed threshold of 0.5, the command picks the threshold with the best validation accuracy and applies it to the test split. summary.md in the same directory is a readable version of the report.
These metrics describe this small synthetic test split. They do not establish survey performance or score calibration. On real data, choose a threshold on validation data for the missed-source and false-positive rates you can accept, then evaluate it once on an independent test split. Precision also depends on how common real sources are in the scored population.

8.7 Score your own cutouts in Python
For cutouts in memory, load the checkpoint and call the model. load_model_from_checkpoint rebuilds the network, loads the saved weights and sets evaluation mode. The triplet model takes a float32 tensor of shape (candidate, channel, y, x), with the channels target, reference, difference. It returns one logit per candidate. Its sigmoid is the model’s real-class score, exposed as probabilities by the inference commands.

import torch
from cuphoton.xscan.training import load_model_from_checkpoint

model, checkpoint, performance = load_model_from_checkpoint(Path("runs/classify-demo"), device=torch.device("cpu"))
cutouts = np.stack([target, reference, difference], axis=1)[split == 2][:6]
with torch.no_grad():
    logits = model(torch.from_numpy(cutouts))
print("p(real):", torch.sigmoid(logits).numpy().round(3))
print("same as infer-real-bogus:", np.allclose(torch.sigmoid(logits).numpy(), probabilities[:6]))

8.8 Handle checkpoints
A checkpoint is a dictionary. model_config holds the network’s shape, model_state its weights, train_config the training configuration and xfit_feature_bundle the identity of optional xFit features.

print(sorted(checkpoint))
config = checkpoint["model_config"]
print(config["input_mode"], config["image_size"], config["embed_dims"])

['model_config', 'model_state', 'train_config', 'xfit_feature_bundle']
triplet 21 [16, 16]


load_model_from_checkpoint passes model_config to build_model and loads model_state into the result. Call build_model(**checkpoint["model_config"]) to build the same network in your own PyTorch code. A checkpoint only works on cutouts with its input mode, size and preprocessing. A wrong size fails late, inside the network. To reject a checkpoint before any model is built, pass a checkpoint_validator, a function that raises ValueError:

def require_triplet(size):
    def check(checkpoint):
        config = checkpoint["model_config"]
        if config["input_mode"] != "triplet" or config["image_size"] != size:
            raise ValueError(f"need a triplet model for {size} px cutouts, got "
                             f"{config['input_mode']} for {config['image_size']} px")
    return check


try:
    load_model_from_checkpoint(Path("runs/classify-demo"), checkpoint_validator=require_triplet(51))
except ValueError as error:
    print("ValueError:", error)

8.11 On a GPU
With the gpu extra, the same commands run on CUDA, which device: auto selects. GPU settings go in the performance section of the YAML file. They are off by default. On a CPU, xScan ignores mixed precision and pinned memory.

import yaml

config = yaml.safe_load(Path("runs/classify-train.yaml").read_text())
config.update(run_name="classify-gpu", device="cuda", performance={
    "amp_dtype": "bf16", "allow_tf32": True, "cudnn_benchmark": True, "num_workers": 2,
    "worker_start_method": "spawn", "pin_memory": True, "persistent_workers": True,
    "non_blocking_transfers": True})
Path("runs/classify-gpu.yaml").write_text(yaml.safe_dump(config, sort_keys=False))

cuphoton xscan train-inada-triplet --config runs/classify-gpu.yaml > runs/classify-gpu.json
For cutouts already on the GPU, predict_tensors scores a contiguous float32 tensor on an explicit CUDA device and returns logits and probabilities on it:

from cuphoton.xscan.training import predict_tensors

device = torch.device("cuda:0")
model, _, performance = load_model_from_checkpoint(Path("runs/classify-gpu"), device=device)
result = predict_tensors(model=model, images=torch.from_numpy(cutouts).to(device), device=device,
                         performance=performance)
print(result["probabilities"].cpu())

predict_fits cuts and scores cutouts straight from aligned FITS images on the GPU, without a dataset directory. It needs CuPy and an explicit CUDA device, and the cutout sides in stamp_shape must be odd. It does not align, subtract or normalize the images.

result = predict_fits(
    model=model, device=device, performance=performance,
    search=FitsPlane("target.fits", hdu=1), template=FitsPlane("reference-aligned.fits", hdu=1),
    difference=FitsPlane("difference.fits", hdu=1),
    centers_yx=[(200, 300), (450, 600)], candidate_ids=["candidate-a", "candidate-b"], stamp_shape=(21, 21),
)
print(result.candidate_ids, result.probabilities)

text:
8.12 What is survey-specific
The array format, the model and the checkpoints are generic. These parts depend on the survey:

Cutout preparation. Size, centering, scaling and masking are your choice. A checkpoint is valid only for cutouts prepared like its training set.
Dataset builders. cuphoton xscan --help lists builders for several surveys’ products, such as data-build-autoscan. Example manifests are in examples/xscan/.
Labels. Define which astrophysical changes count as real for your task. The label guard rejects placeholder labels from survey smoke datasets and survey object IDs that appear in two splits; it cannot verify that a human label is scientifically correct.
Thresholds and calibration. Choose the threshold on a representative validation split, and check performance and score calibration on held-out data with the class balance and observing conditions you expect to encounter.

8.13 Troubleshooting

ERROR: [Errno 17] File exists: '.../runs/classify-demo'

Each training run needs a new directory. Change run_name or delete the old run.

ERROR: refusing to train with group leakage across train/validation/test splits, or refusing to train on labels that are not real-bogus usable: label_source_untrusted

The label guard failed. Run data-check-training-labels and fix the listed metadata. A label_source that is empty or contains “placeholder” or “unlabeled” is untrusted.

RuntimeError: The expanded size of the tensor (676) must match the existing size (121)

The cutouts differ in size from the checkpoint’s image_size. Use a checkpoint_validator to catch this at load time.

ValueError: triplet model expects 3-channel stacked input

Stack the channels target, reference and difference, in that order. A pair model takes the first two.

9.1 Make a sample pair
The cuPhoton checkout ships an end-to-end pipeline in examples/transient-chain/. It takes a target image and its reference from FITS files to a catalog of candidates, each with a position, a flux, their error bars and, with a classifier checkpoint, a real-or-bogus score. Each GPU worker keeps the main image calculations on the device. Astropy reads begin on the host, and WCS work, optional host star finding, diagnostics and final catalog columns can cross the host/device boundary. Use it to run the whole pipeline on your own images instead of calling each module as in Chapter 2. The chain needs an NVIDIA GPU. Its configuration, input checks and file loaders run on a CPU, and this page runs them on the sample pair.
The worker runs these steps for each target image:
You need:
The block below writes sample/reference.fits and sample/target.fits, the pair of Chapter 2.
Create the sample pair (NumPy and Astropy only)
# Writes sample/reference.fits and sample/target.fits: two synthetic star fields
# of the same sky on different pixel grids, with different blur and sky level.
# The target also holds one new source and one star three times brighter.
# Noise is independent Gaussian noise with variance expected_image / gain;
# this teaching sample has no read noise, saturation, or detector artifacts.
from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np
from astropy.io import fits
from astropy.wcs import WCS

rng = np.random.default_rng(7)


def make_wcs(shape, scale_arcsec, rotation_deg, crpix_shift):
    w = WCS(naxis=2)
    w.wcs.ctype = ["RA---TAN", "DEC--TAN"]
    w.wcs.crval = [150.0, 2.0]
    w.wcs.crpix = [shape[1] / 2 + crpix_shift[0], shape[0] / 2 + crpix_shift[1]]
    c, s = np.cos(np.radians(rotation_deg)), np.sin(np.radians(rotation_deg))
    w.wcs.cd = scale_arcsec / 3600 * np.array([[-c, s], [s, c]])
    return w


def render(shape, wcs, ra, dec, flux, sigma, sky, gain):
    x, y = wcs.world_to_pixel_values(ra, dec)
    yy, xx = np.mgrid[: shape[0], : shape[1]]
    image = np.full(shape, sky, dtype=float)
    for xi, yi, fi in zip(x, y, flux):
        image += fi / (2 * np.pi * sigma**2) * np.exp(-((xx - xi) ** 2 + (yy - yi) ** 2) / (2 * sigma**2))
    return rng.normal(image, np.sqrt(image / gain)).astype(np.float32)


ra = 150.0 + rng.uniform(-0.016, 0.016, 150)
dec = 2.0 + rng.uniform(-0.016, 0.016, 150)
flux = 10 ** rng.uniform(2.5, 4.5, 150)
target_flux = np.r_[3 * flux[0], flux[1:], 4000.0]  # star 0 brightens; one new source
target_ra, target_dec = np.r_[ra, 150.004], np.r_[dec, 2.003]

Path("sample").mkdir(exist_ok=True)
for name, shape, wcs, sky_coords, fl, sigma, sky, gain in [
    ("reference", (300, 300), make_wcs((300, 300), 0.26, 0.0, (0, 0)), (ra, dec), flux, 1.2, 100.0, 8.0),
    ("target", (256, 256), make_wcs((256, 256), 0.27, 3.0, (4.3, -2.7)), (target_ra, target_dec), target_flux, 1.8, 120.0, 2.0),
]:
    header = wcs.to_header()
    header["GAIN"] = (gain, "electrons per data number (DN)")
    header["PSFSIG"] = (sigma, "Gaussian PSF sigma [px]")
    fits.writeto(f"sample/{name}.fits", render(shape, wcs, *sky_coords, fl, sigma, sky, gain), header, overwrite=True)
The correlation term of the chain’s error budget requires a locally translation-only mapping. When that term is active, a rotated or rescaled grid gives undefined error bars (Section 9.11.1). Write a second target that keeps the reference’s pixel scale and orientation, with the same two changes:
wcs = make_wcs((256, 256), 0.26, 0.0, (4.3, 6.3))  # the reference's scale, no rotation, shifted by a few pixels
header = wcs.to_header()
header["GAIN"], header["PSFSIG"] = 2.0, 1.8
image = render((256, 256), wcs, target_ra, target_dec, target_flux, 1.8, 120.0, 2.0)
fits.writeto("sample/chain-target.fits", image, header, overwrite=True)

9.11 Read the catalog and the summary
The local run writes out/items/<item>/catalog.parquet and summary.json for each item, and out/catalog.parquet with the rows of all items. Dragon and MPI write the same files under <output-dir>/<name>/. Every item writes the same columns with the same types, also when it finds no candidates. Print the column count, the flux columns and the error terms:

from cuphoton.xfit import GaussianDipoleModel
from transient_chain import catalog

columns = catalog.schema(GaussianDipoleModel((51, 51)).parameter_names)  # the worker's dipole model
print(len(columns), "columns")
print([name for name in columns if name.startswith("psf_flux")])
for term, meaning in catalog.BUDGET_TERMS.items():
    print(f"{term:7} {meaning}")

93 columns
['psf_flux', 'psf_flux_err_fit', 'psf_flux_err', 'psf_flux_err_corr', 'psf_flux_err_kfit', 'psf_flux_err_kmatch', 'psf_flux_err_mis']
corr    correlated reference noise through the resampling and the kernel
kfit    the kernel fit's own uncertainty
kmatch  kernel mismatch times the reference flux (psf_flux only; 0 for positions)
mis     residual misalignment (0 for psf_flux)


The columns you are most likely to use:







Column
Meaning




candidate_id
cu-<exposure_id>-<ccd_id>-<index>


x, y
rounded hotspot centroid on the target grid, in zero-based pixels


ra, dec
sky position in degrees, from the target header WCS at (x, y), rather than the fitted source position


sign
sign of the hotspot’s peak residual: +1 for a positive excursion, -1 for a negative excursion


source_x, source_y
position of the measured source in pixels, relative to (x, y)


psf_flux
difference flux at the source, in target image units; normally forced PSF (point spread function) photometry. It requires a variance plane and an independent PSF width. Without that width, an accepted one-lobe fit supplies its fitted flux; other rows are NaN


fit_model
"dipole", or "single" for a candidate refit with one lobe


quality_flags
bits of cuphoton.xfit.DipoleQualityFlag, 0 when none is set


probability, decision
classifier output, NaN and false without a checkpoint




9.11.1 Error bars
The budget covers center_x, center_y, positive_x, positive_y and, when forced photometry runs, psf_flux. For each computed quantity q, use <q>_err: the quadrature sum of <q>_err_fit and the available terms above. It is NaN where fewer than half the pixels in a required window are usable, the correlation factor is undefined, or the total uncertainty is non-finite. A center needs both lobe windows to pass.
With the budget enabled, uq_valid means that every computed budget quantity has a defined error. It does not certify that every term was available, that the source model is appropriate, or that unavailable PSF photometry has a valid error. If a one-lobe fitted flux stands in for missing forced photometry, it keeps its fit-only error. Inspect summary.json for excluded terms and quality_flags for fit problems.
source_x_err and source_y_err normally copy the positive_* bars. For a fading candidate identified by the lobe-support flags whose one-lobe refit was not accepted, source_* instead selects the dipole’s negative lobe and its position errors are NaN: the budget was computed for the positive lobe.
When corr is active, its factor is undefined where the grid mapping between the two images is not locally a shift, for example a reference that is rotated or has a different pixel scale. The affected computed quantities get NaN error bars and uq_valid is false. summary.json counts them under uq.undefined_factor, and those on a rotated grid under uq.rotated_grid. The example’s README explains why. This page’s sample target shares the reference’s pixel scale and orientation for that reason.
After a GPU run, inspect the rows and read how the item’s bars were built. This block needs a finished run and is not run here.

table = pd.read_parquet("out/catalog.parquet")
columns = ["x", "y", "fit_model", "quality_flags", "psf_flux", "psf_flux_err", "source_x_err", "uq_valid"]
print(table[columns].to_string())

summary = json.loads(Path("out/items/S1-v1/summary.json").read_text())
print(summary["candidates"], summary["psf_sigma_source"], summary["uq_terms"])
if summary["uq"] is not None:  # null when there are no candidates
    print(summary["uq"]["excluded"])  # each term left out, with the reason

A candidate can have a finite flux error and still have uq_valid=False because a position error is undefined. Check quality_flags and fit_model before quoting a position. The one-lobe refit is attempted only when exactly one lobe is unsupported, and its result replaces the dipole position only when the refit covariance is valid. Rows with both lobes unsupported keep their dipole values and need further inspection.
psf_sigma_source reports where the PSF width came from. If uq.excluded reports mis: no misalignment model, inspect diagnostics.align.refine.misalignment.reason for the cause. These GPU result fields are described from the implementation; this page’s executable examples validate the CPU setup and input loading.
summary.json also records the reader each file took (diagnostics.read.receipts), the time per stage (timings_sec) and the bytes copied to the host (transfers).

text:
10.1 Make a sample pair
The xFit measurements on this page report uncertainties from a fitted covariance or a fixed-PSF flux estimate. xRep resamples your variance planes, xPois propagates them into the difference image, and xFit uses them as weights. Use this page to assess correlated noise, read the transient chain’s error budget, and check error bars on your own data. Failed or unsupported uncertainty estimates can be NaN.
You need:
The block below writes the pair of Chapter 2. The target is rotated by 3 degrees against the reference and has slightly larger pixels.
Create the sample pair (NumPy and Astropy only)
# Writes sample/reference.fits and sample/target.fits: two synthetic star fields
# of the same sky on different pixel grids, with different blur and sky level.
# The target also holds one new source and one star three times brighter.
# Noise is independent Gaussian noise with variance expected_image / gain;
# this teaching sample has no read noise, saturation, or detector artifacts.
from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np
from astropy.io import fits
from astropy.wcs import WCS

rng = np.random.default_rng(7)


def make_wcs(shape, scale_arcsec, rotation_deg, crpix_shift):
    w = WCS(naxis=2)
    w.wcs.ctype = ["RA---TAN", "DEC--TAN"]
    w.wcs.crval = [150.0, 2.0]
    w.wcs.crpix = [shape[1] / 2 + crpix_shift[0], shape[0] / 2 + crpix_shift[1]]
    c, s = np.cos(np.radians(rotation_deg)), np.sin(np.radians(rotation_deg))
    w.wcs.cd = scale_arcsec / 3600 * np.array([[-c, s], [s, c]])
    return w


def render(shape, wcs, ra, dec, flux, sigma, sky, gain):
    x, y = wcs.world_to_pixel_values(ra, dec)
    yy, xx = np.mgrid[: shape[0], : shape[1]]
    image = np.full(shape, sky, dtype=float)
    for xi, yi, fi in zip(x, y, flux):
        image += fi / (2 * np.pi * sigma**2) * np.exp(-((xx - xi) ** 2 + (yy - yi) ** 2) / (2 * sigma**2))
    return rng.normal(image, np.sqrt(image / gain)).astype(np.float32)


ra = 150.0 + rng.uniform(-0.016, 0.016, 150)
dec = 2.0 + rng.uniform(-0.016, 0.016, 150)
flux = 10 ** rng.uniform(2.5, 4.5, 150)
target_flux = np.r_[3 * flux[0], flux[1:], 4000.0]  # star 0 brightens; one new source
target_ra, target_dec = np.r_[ra, 150.004], np.r_[dec, 2.003]

Path("sample").mkdir(exist_ok=True)
for name, shape, wcs, sky_coords, fl, sigma, sky, gain in [
    ("reference", (300, 300), make_wcs((300, 300), 0.26, 0.0, (0, 0)), (ra, dec), flux, 1.2, 100.0, 8.0),
    ("target", (256, 256), make_wcs((256, 256), 0.27, 3.0, (4.3, -2.7)), (target_ra, target_dec), target_flux, 1.8, 120.0, 2.0),
]:
    header = wcs.to_header()
    header["GAIN"] = (gain, "electrons per data number (DN)")
    header["PSFSIG"] = (sigma, "Gaussian PSF sigma [px]")
    fits.writeto(f"sample/{name}.fits", render(shape, wcs, *sky_coords, fl, sigma, sky, gain), header, overwrite=True)

text:
10.2 Follow the noise through the pipeline
These calls propagate and use the per-pixel variance planes:









Step
Call
Noise it returns
Guide




Your input
a variance plane per image
the expected squared error of each pixel, in squared image units
Chapter 3


Align
reproject_masked_array (xRep)
the reference variance on the target grid, through the squared interpolation weights
Chapter 5


Subtract
standardize_constant_kernel_residual (xPois)
marginal_residual_variance, the target variance plus the reference variance convolved with the squared kernel, and standardized_residual, the difference over its square root
Chapter 6


Measure
fit_single_sources, forced_psf_photometry, fit_dipoles (xFit)
the errors of each call, such as flux_error, covariance, standard_errors and uncertainty_valid
Chapter 7



These variance planes store one variance per pixel, without covariances between pixels. The subtraction diagnostic below treats the fitted kernel as fixed, and the xFit errors initially assume independent pixels. The blocks align and subtract as in Chapter 7, and print the median variance after each step.

import numpy as np
from astropy.wcs import WCS
from cuphoton.core.fits_io import read_fits_images
from cuphoton.xrep import BBox, ReprojectionSpec, make_wcs_pair_transform, prepare_reprojection, reproject_masked_array

target_read, reference_read = (read_fits_images(f"sample/{name}.fits", [0]) for name in ("target", "reference"))
target, reference = (r.arrays[0].astype(np.float64) for r in (target_read, reference_read))
target_header, reference_header = target_read.infos[0].header, reference_read.infos[0].header
target_variance = np.clip(target, 0, None) / target_header["GAIN"]  # your own variance planes go here
reference_variance = np.clip(reference, 0, None) / reference_header["GAIN"]
spec = ReprojectionSpec(mapping=make_wcs_pair_transform(WCS(target_header), WCS(reference_header)),
                        output_bbox=BBox(0, 0, target.shape[1], target.shape[0]))  # (x, y) origin, then the size
prepared = prepare_reprojection(spec, source_shape=reference.shape)
no_bad_pixels = np.zeros(reference.shape, dtype=bool)
aligned = reproject_masked_array(reference, reference_variance, no_bad_pixels, spec, backend="cpu", prepared=prepared)


from cuphoton.xpois import (GaussianBasisComponent, identify_residual_hotspots, solve_constant_kernel,
                            standardize_constant_kernel_residual)

basis = [GaussianBasisComponent(0.7, 4), GaussianBasisComponent(1.4, 2), GaussianBasisComponent(2.8, 2)]
fit = solve_constant_kernel(aligned.image, target, basis, kernel_shape=(19, 19),
                            variance=target_variance, background_degree=1, backend="cpu")
noise = standardize_constant_kernel_residual(fit.residual, kernel=fit.kernel, target_variance=target_variance,
                                             reference_variance=aligned.variance)
difference, difference_variance, inside = fit.residual, noise.marginal_residual_variance, noise.valid_mask
for name, plane in [("reference", reference_variance), ("reference, aligned", aligned.variance),
                    ("reference, through the kernel", noise.propagated_reference_variance),
                    ("target", target_variance), ("difference", difference_variance)]:
    print(f"{name:30s} median variance {np.nanmedian(plane):6.2f}")

reference                      median variance  12.52
reference, aligned             median variance  11.54
reference, through the kernel  median variance   0.49
target                         median variance  60.29
difference                     median variance  60.78


In this example, alignment and the kernel reduce the reference’s median variance by combining input pixels. Resampling and convolution also correlate neighboring output pixels, which a per-pixel variance does not describe. The variance need not decrease for other interpolation weights, pixel-area scalings or kernels.

text:
10.3 Measure the candidates
Find the two candidates and fit them with xFit. The window, \(2\lceil 5\sigma\rceil + 1\) pixels for a PSF (point spread function) width \(\sigma\), is the one the transient chain uses.

from cuphoton.xfit import fit_single_sources
from cuphoton.xpois import window_stamps

regions = identify_residual_hotspots(noise.standardized_residual, robust_sigma=1.0, max_regions=None)
candidates = np.array([region["peak_yx"][::-1] for region in regions], dtype=float)  # (x, y)
psf_sigma = target_header["PSFSIG"]
size = 2 * int(np.ceil(5 * psf_sigma)) + 1
cutout_variance = window_stamps(difference_variance, candidates, size)
sources = fit_single_sources(window_stamps(difference, candidates, size), cutout_variance,
                             np.zeros((len(candidates), 2)), psf_sigma, mask=np.isfinite(cutout_variance),
                             sign=1)  # both candidates brightened
print("window", size, "px, uncertainty_valid", sources.uncertainty_valid)
print("flux error      ", sources.flux_error.round(1))
print("x position error", sources.position_error_x.round(4))

window 19 px, uncertainty_valid [ True  True]
flux error       [113.5  70.6]
x position error [0.0194 0.0393]


The errors come from the fit covariance and are NaN where uncertainty_valid is false.
title: 10  Uncertainty Quantification

text:
10.4 Correct for correlated noise
A fixed-PSF flux is a weighted sum of difference pixels; a fitted position can be approximated by one after linearizing the fit. The correlation factor \(f\) is the variance of that sum including covariance, divided by the variance predicted from independent pixels. Multiply its error bar by \(\sqrt{f}\) to account for that covariance. The factor depends on the estimator’s weights and can be below one, especially for signed derivative weights.

10.4.1 Measure the factor at empty positions
empty_positions picks pixels more than one window from every candidate and every loud pixel. empirical_correlation_factor divides the weighted sum of the difference at each by its predicted error, and returns the squared robust spread (1.4826 times the median absolute deviation) of the ratios. psf_weights builds a Gaussian PSF and its derivatives. These approximate flux and position weights for a symmetric PSF in uniform noise; inverse-variance weighting, masks and joint parameter fitting change the actual weights.

from cuphoton.xpois import empirical_correlation_factor, empty_positions, psf_weights

# loud: pixels more than 5 robust sigmas from the median of the difference
empty, _ = empty_positions(inside, exclude_xy=candidates, window=size, count=500, loud=(difference, 5.0))
weights = np.stack([psf_weights(psf_sigma, size), psf_weights(psf_sigma, size, derivative="x"),
                    psf_weights(psf_sigma, size, derivative="y")])  # a flux, an x and a y position
measured = empirical_correlation_factor(difference, difference_variance, weights, empty)
n = measured.positions_used
standard_error = measured.factor * np.sqrt(2 / (0.3675 * (n - 1)))  # as the transient chain computes it
print(f"{n} positions. Factors for the flux, x and y: {measured.factor.round(3)}; nominal SE {standard_error.round(3)}")

415 positions. Factors for the flux, x and y: [1.138 1.065 1.026]; nominal SE [0.131 0.122 0.118]


The printed standard error is the chain’s approximation for independent Gaussian samples. Empty windows can overlap and share noise, so increasing their count does not necessarily add independent information. Use separated positions or repeated independent images to assess the sampling uncertainty.


10.4.2 Apply the factor
The following scaling illustrates an approximate adjustment to the fitted errors. A factor measured with background PSF weights need not describe a bright source or a joint nonlinear fit exactly. For a particular estimator, use its weights and variance, as the forced-photometry example below does. Flooring the factor at one is the chain’s conservative policy, not a mathematical bound on \(f\).

f_flux, f_x, f_y = np.maximum(measured.factor, 1.0)
print("flux error      ", sources.flux_error.round(1), "->", (sources.flux_error * np.sqrt(f_flux)).round(1))
print("x position error", sources.position_error_x.round(4), "->", (sources.position_error_x * np.sqrt(f_x)).round(4))

flux error       [113.5  70.6] -> [121.1  75.3]
x position error [0.0194 0.0393] -> [0.02   0.0405]




10.4.3 Compute the factor in closed form
correlation_factor estimates \(f\) at each position from the kernel, both variance planes and the interpolation weights that xRep applied there, which resampling_weights_at returns. It assumes independent target and reference input noise, a fixed kernel, and locally stationary resampling. It infers a local reference-noise level from the resampled variance; this is not exact propagation of an arbitrary spatially varying input covariance. Pass resampling_weights_at the prepared mapping of the alignment.

from cuphoton.xpois import correlation_factor
from cuphoton.xrep import resampling_weights_at

taps = resampling_weights_at(spec, candidates[:, 0], candidates[:, 1], prepared=prepared, source_shape=reference.shape)
closed = correlation_factor(weights[0], kernel=fit.kernel, target_variance=target_variance,
                            reference_variance=aligned.variance, resampling_weights=taps.weights,
                            positions=candidates, residual_variance=difference_variance,
                            is_translation=taps.is_translation)
print("is_translation", taps.is_translation, "factor", closed.factor, "n_rotated", closed.n_rotated)
print("local Jacobian, reference pixels per target pixel:\n", taps.jacobian[0].round(3))

is_translation [False False] factor [nan nan] n_rotated 2
local Jacobian, reference pixels per target pixel:
 [[ 1.037 -0.054]
 [ 0.054  1.037]]


The closed form is supported only where the mapping between the grids is locally a shift. is_translation is false where the local Jacobian, the change of reference pixel per target pixel, differs from the identity by more than 1e-3. Here it shows the rotation and the change of pixel scale. On such a pair, a measured factor can still diagnose the noise. When the chain’s correlation term is active, an undefined closed-form factor leaves the affected computed error bars NaN; the measured factor does not replace it (Section 9.11.1).
Write a target that only a shift separates from the reference, and subtract it. make_wcs and render come from the sample-pair block.

shift_wcs = make_wcs((256, 256), 0.26, 0.0, (4.3, 6.3))  # the reference's scale and orientation
shifted = render((256, 256), shift_wcs, target_ra, target_dec, target_flux, psf_sigma, 120.0,
                 target_header["GAIN"]).astype(np.float64)
shifted_variance = np.clip(shifted, 0, None) / target_header["GAIN"]
shift_spec = ReprojectionSpec(mapping=make_wcs_pair_transform(shift_wcs, WCS(reference_header)),
                              output_bbox=BBox(0, 0, 256, 256))
shift_prepared = prepare_reprojection(shift_spec, source_shape=reference.shape)
shift_aligned = reproject_masked_array(reference, reference_variance, no_bad_pixels, shift_spec, backend="cpu",
                                       prepared=shift_prepared)
shift_fit = solve_constant_kernel(shift_aligned.image, shifted, basis, kernel_shape=(19, 19),
                                  variance=shifted_variance, background_degree=1, backend="cpu")
shift_noise = standardize_constant_kernel_residual(shift_fit.residual, kernel=shift_fit.kernel,
                                                   target_variance=shifted_variance,
                                                   reference_variance=shift_aligned.variance)

Read the resampling weights at empty positions of the new difference:

shift_regions = identify_residual_hotspots(shift_noise.standardized_residual, robust_sigma=1.0, max_regions=None)
shift_candidates = np.array([region["peak_yx"][::-1] for region in shift_regions], dtype=float)
shift_empty, _ = empty_positions(shift_noise.valid_mask, exclude_xy=shift_candidates, window=size, count=500,
                                 loud=(shift_fit.residual, 5.0))
shift_taps = resampling_weights_at(shift_spec, shift_empty[:, 0], shift_empty[:, 1], prepared=shift_prepared,
                                   source_shape=reference.shape)
print("is_translation everywhere", bool(shift_taps.is_translation.all()))

is_translation everywhere True


Compute both factors at those positions. With weights of shape (N, q, s, s), one call returns q factors per position.

shift_closed = correlation_factor(np.broadcast_to(weights, (len(shift_empty),) + weights.shape),
                                  kernel=shift_fit.kernel, target_variance=shifted_variance,
                                  reference_variance=shift_aligned.variance, resampling_weights=shift_taps.weights,
                                  positions=shift_empty, residual_variance=shift_noise.marginal_residual_variance,
                                  is_translation=shift_taps.is_translation)
shift_measured = empirical_correlation_factor(shift_fit.residual, shift_noise.marginal_residual_variance,
                                              weights, shift_empty)
shift_error = shift_measured.factor * np.sqrt(2 / (0.3675 * (shift_measured.positions_used - 1)))
print("closed form, median", np.nanmedian(shift_closed.factor, axis=0).round(3))
print("measured           ", shift_measured.factor.round(3), "nominal SE", shift_error.round(3))

closed form, median [1.129 1.081 1.081]
measured            [1.069 1.237 1.222] nominal SE [0.123 0.143 0.141]


The closed form models the resampling and the kernel, but omits correlations already present in a coadd (a stack of resampled exposures). The chain accepts a measured factor when it exceeds one and the median closed form by more than two nominal standard errors. It then raises a candidate’s factor only if the candidate’s closed form is finite and smaller than that measured value.

section: 10.5 Read the transient chain’s error budget
text:
10.5 Read the transient chain’s error budget
The transient chain (Chapter 9) runs these calls and adds three more terms. For each computed quantity q, one of center_x, center_y, positive_x, positive_y and psf_flux, it writes the error bar <q>_err and each term in its own column. The flux budget is available only when forced photometry ran:
<q>_err = sqrt(fit^2 + corr^2 + kfit^2 + kmatch^2 + mis^2)



Table 10.1: The terms of the chain’s error budget, from docs/uncertainty-quantification.md and transient_chain/uq.py.












Term
Column
What it adds
Applies to
Needs




fit
<q>_err_fit
xFit’s error, weighted by the target variance plane
all five
the fit. Without a target variance plane, xFit scales the covariance by the reduced chi-square


corr
<q>_err_corr
the reference’s noise and its correlation, <q>_err_fit * sqrt(max(f, 1) - 1), with f relative to the target variance
all five
target and reference variance planes, and a PSF width


kfit
<q>_err_kfit
the uncertainty of the fitted kernel and background, largest on a bright reference source
all five
a target variance plane, a PSF width and uq.kernel_fit: true


kmatch
<q>_err_kmatch
reference flux the kernel did not match, eta times the matched reference flux at the source
psf_flux, 0 for positions
a target variance plane, a PSF width and at least 5 stars matched by the refine stage


mis
<q>_err_mis
the alignment error left after the refine stage
positions, 0 for psf_flux
a misalignment model: align.refine: true, an affine refinement, a star finder other than daofind, and a reference that the chain reprojects or mosaics onto the target grid


sky
sky_err_arcsec
the absolute sky astrometry of the exposure
reported apart, never added to <q>_err
uq.sky_astrometry_arcsec and uq.sky_astrometry_source






A term without its inputs is left out; that does not establish that its physical contribution is zero. Check the recorded exclusions when interpreting the result. The uq block of the configuration sets the budget:








Key
Default
Effect




uq.enabled
true
false sets every <q>_err to <q>_err_fit and every other term to 0


uq.kernel_fit
true
computes the kfit term


uq.measure_correlation
true
measures the correlation factor at empty positions of each exposure


uq.correlation_positions
1000
the number of empty positions for that measurement, at least 20


uq.max_lobe_reach_px
32
the largest center-to-lobe distance that keeps a center error bar


uq.single_source_refit
true
refits a candidate with one unsupported lobe with the one-lobe model


uq.sky_astrometry_arcsec, uq.sky_astrometry_source
null
set together. They are copied to sky_err_arcsec and sky_err_source



With the budget enabled, quote <q>_err. It is NaN when its fit error is nonfinite, its required window is unusable or its active correlation factor is undefined. A window needs at least half its pixels usable, and center estimates require both lobes within the configured reach. uq_valid covers the quantities that the budget computed; it does not certify every catalog output or the availability of all terms. With uq.enabled: false, the flag is set true without those checks. The block below, which needs a finished run (Section 9.11.1), rebuilds an error bar without one term.

import json
import pandas as pd

table = pd.read_parquet("out/catalog.parquet")
rows = table[table["uq_valid"]]
terms = ["fit", "corr", "kfit", "kmatch", "mis"]
print(rows[["psf_flux", "psf_flux_err"] + [f"psf_flux_err_{term}" for term in terms]])
without_kfit = np.sqrt(sum(rows[f"psf_flux_err_{term}"] ** 2 for term in terms if term != "kfit"))

summary = json.load(open("out/items/S1-v1/summary.json"))
print(summary["uq_terms"])
uq = summary["uq"]
if uq is not None:  # no budget summary when no candidates were found
    print(uq["excluded"])
    correlation = uq.get("correlation")
    if correlation is not None:  # absent when disabled or unavailable
        print(correlation["source"])

Field

section: 10.6 Check your error bars with injected sources
text:
10.6 Check your error bars with injected sources
Inject sources of known flux into your difference image and measure them as you measure your candidates. A source’s pull is its measured minus true flux, over its error bar. Unbiased estimates with calibrated errors should have pulls centered near zero with width near one in the tested regime.
This example tests fixed-position forced photometry conditional on an already fitted subtraction. It does not test detection and selection, errors in fitted positions, or the effect of injected sources on alignment and kernel fitting. For those, inject into the input exposures and rerun the relevant stages.
The correction matters when the reference’s noise is a large part of the difference image’s noise, and xRep resampled the reference onto the target grid. The sample reference is much deeper than the target, and its correction is small. Make a second reference as noisy as the target, on the same grid, and subtract it from the shifted target:

gain = target_header["GAIN"]
# the sample reference's stars, grid and PSF, with the target's sky level and gain
shallow = render(reference.shape, WCS(reference_header), ra, dec, flux, reference_header["PSFSIG"], 120.0,
                 gain).astype(np.float64)
shallow_variance = np.clip(shallow, 0, None) / gain
shallow_aligned = reproject_masked_array(shallow, shallow_variance, no_bad_pixels, shift_spec, backend="cpu",
                                         prepared=shift_prepared)
shallow_fit = solve_constant_kernel(shallow_aligned.image, shifted, basis, kernel_shape=(19, 19),
                                    variance=shifted_variance, background_degree=1, backend="cpu")
shallow_noise = standardize_constant_kernel_residual(shallow_fit.residual, kernel=shallow_fit.kernel,
                                                     target_variance=shifted_variance,
                                                     reference_variance=shallow_aligned.variance)
print(f"median variance: deep reference {np.median(reference_variance):.1f}, "
      f"shallow reference {np.median(shallow_variance):.1f}, target {np.median(shifted_variance):.1f}")

median variance: deep reference 12.5, shallow reference 60.1, target 60.3


Place one source per cell of an 11 pixel grid where the window is empty, adding a Gaussian approximation to photon noise. Both pairs get the same sources and noise. Their measurement windows overlap, so the pulls are not independent samples.

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)  # a new seed for the injection
all_empty, _ = empty_positions(shift_noise.valid_mask, exclude_xy=shift_candidates, window=size,
                               count=shifted.size, loud=(shift_fit.residual, 5.0))
is_empty = np.zeros(shifted.shape, dtype=bool)
is_empty[all_empty[:, 1].astype(int), all_empty[:, 0].astype(int)] = True
gy, gx = np.mgrid[size:shifted.shape[0] - size:11, size:shifted.shape[1] - size:11]
keep = is_empty[gy, gx]
true_xy = np.column_stack([gx[keep], gy[keep]]) + rng.uniform(-0.5, 0.5, (keep.sum(), 2))  # (x, y)
true_flux = rng.uniform(500, 3000, len(true_xy))
half = size // 2
rows = np.rint(true_xy[:, 1]).astype(int)[:, None, None] + np.arange(-half, half + 1)[:, None]
cols = np.rint(true_xy[:, 0]).astype(int)[:, None, None] + np.arange(-half, half + 1)
model = np.zeros_like(shifted)
np.add.at(model, (rows, cols), true_flux[:, None, None] * psf_weights(psf_sigma, size, offset=true_xy - np.rint(true_xy)))
source_noise = rng.normal(0.0, np.sqrt(model / gain))
print(len(true_xy), "sources")

299 sources


injection_test injects the sources into one difference and measures them with forced_flux_at at their true positions, without estimating a local sky. It adjusts each flux error with the closed-form factor for that forced estimator’s inverse-variance weights. It also measures the background factor at the empty positions.

from cuphoton.xpois import forced_flux_at

source_taps = resampling_weights_at(shift_spec, true_xy[:, 0], true_xy[:, 1], prepared=shift_prepared,
                                    source_shape=reference.shape)


def injection_test(aligned_reference, subtraction, subtraction_noise):
    injected = subtraction.residual + model + source_noise
    injected_variance = subtraction_noise.marginal_residual_variance + model / gain
    photometry = forced_flux_at(injected, true_xy, psf_sigma, window=size, variance=injected_variance, local_sky=False)
    pull = (photometry.flux - true_flux) / photometry.flux_error
    flux_weights = (psf_weights(psf_sigma, size, offset=true_xy - np.rint(true_xy))
                    / window_stamps(injected_variance, true_xy, size))  # the weights of the forced flux
    closed = correlation_factor(flux_weights, kernel=subtraction.kernel, target_variance=shifted_variance + model / gain,
                                reference_variance=aligned_reference.variance, resampling_weights=source_taps.weights,
                                positions=true_xy, residual_variance=injected_variance,
                                is_translation=source_taps.is_translation).factor
    measured = empirical_correlation_factor(subtraction.residual, subtraction_noise.marginal_residual_variance,
                                            weights[0], shift_empty)
    return pull, pull / np.sqrt(np.maximum(closed, 1.0)), closed, measured

Run it on both pairs and compare:

results = {"deep reference": injection_test(shift_aligned, shift_fit, shift_noise),
           "shallow reference": injection_test(shallow_aligned, shallow_fit, shallow_noise)}
print(f"{'':18s} {'measured factor':>16s} {'closed form':>12s} {'fit-only width':>15s} {'corrected width':>16s}")
for name, (pull, corrected, closed, measured) in results.items():
    width = [f"{p.std(ddof=1):.2f}" for p in (pull, corrected)]
    print(f"{name:18s} {measured.factor:16.2f} {np.median(closed):12.2f} {width[0]:>15s} "
          f"{width[1]:>16s}")

                    measured factor  closed form  fit-only width  corrected width
deep reference                 1.07         1.10            1.01             0.96
shallow reference              1.54         1.45            1.20             0.99


Here the closed form, a median over the sources, is smaller than the background measurement: the sources add independent photon noise, and their inverse-variance weights differ from the background weights. With the shallow reference, the fit-only pulls are wider than one and the corrected pulls sit nearer one. With the deep reference, the correction is small. Figure 10.1 shows both cases; these overlapping samples do not establish an independent-sample significance for the width difference.


Plotting code
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.5, 2.8), sharey=True)
bins, grid = np.linspace(-4, 4, 21), np.linspace(-4, 4, 200)
for ax, (name, (pull, corrected, _, _)) in zip(axes, results.items()):
    ax.hist(corrected, bins=bins, density=True, color="#2A78D6", alpha=0.8, label="corrected")
    ax.hist(pull, bins=bins, density=True, histtype="step", color="0.5", lw=1.5, label="fit error alone")
    ax.plot(grid, np.exp(-grid**2 / 2) / np.sqrt(2 * np.pi), color="#EB6834", lw=2, label="unit normal")
    ax.set_title(name.capitalize(), fontsize=9)
    ax.set_xlabel("Pull")
axes[0].set_ylabel("Density")
axes[1].legend(frameon=False, fontsize=7)
fig.text(1, 1, "Synthetic data, for demonstration only", ha="right", va="bottom",
         fontsize=7, style="italic", color="0.4", transform=fig.transFigure)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()








Figure 10.1: Pulls of the injected sources, measured minus true flux over the flux error, for the deep sample reference (left) and a reference as noisy as the target (right). Gray outline: with the fit error alone. Blue bars: with the closed-form correlation factor applied. Orange line: a unit normal for comparison with unbiased Gaussian errors. With the noisy reference, the fit-only pulls spread wider than the unit normal. Synthetic data, for demonstration only.





Read the result like this:








Result
What it means
What to change




width near one, mean near zero
the errors are consistent with the scatter in this test
test other fluxes, positions and observing conditions


width above one
possible missing variance, model error or outliers
check covariance, gain, read noise, the PSF and the background; compare the chain’s full budget


width below one
possible excess variance or effects of selection and shared noise
check for noise counted twice and measure the factor before applying it. A factor near one means little net correction for those weights, not proof that a variance plane contains covariance


mean away from zero
the fluxes are biased, for example by a wrong PSF width or a background left in the difference
measure the PSF width from your stars, and check the background fit



For repeated exposures of one field, repeat_catalogs.py runs the same test on the chain’s catalogs, without injections. Run it from the root of your cuPhoton checkout:
python examples/transient-chain/repeat_catalogs.py out/items/*/catalog.parquet --out repeat.json
It scores <q>_err with and without each term. Reusing a reference correlates measurements across exposures: a common noise contribution can cancel in their differences, although changing PSFs or weights changes how it projects into each measurement. A score below one can therefore coexist with appropriate errors for individual measurements. A bias that every exposure shares passes the test unseen. The repeat test explains its report.

text:
10.7 Limits
The error bars do not cover these cases:

A PSF model that does not match the data. A wrong width biases a forced flux, and the flux error does not include the bias.
The absolute sky astrometry (how well pixels map to sky positions), which the chain reports in sky_err_arcsec.
Errors that are not small next to the PSF width and the lobe separation. The error bars are first order.
Wrong variance planes. The fit term and the closed form assume that the planes describe the pixel noise.
Unmatched reference light in a position. The kmatch term covers the flux only.

text:
11.1 Make the frames
xImage makes one sharp image from many registered frames with known PSFs (point spread functions: the blur pattern of a point of light in each frame). It fits one nonnegative scene that, blurred by each frame’s PSF, matches every frame within its noise. Use it when you have several exposures of the same field on one pixel grid, each with its own blur and noise. xImage runs on PyTorch, on a CPU or a CUDA GPU. Each workflow reads a bundle of arrays and a YAML configuration, then writes a run directory with a receipt.
You need:
The block below makes three noisy 64 by 64 frames of three point sources. Each frame has its own Gaussian PSF, 0.8, 1.0 and 1.2 pixels wide. These are the same arrays that the repository’s examples/ximage/make_synthetic_bundle.py writes.
import numpy as np
from scipy.signal import convolve2d

scene = np.full((64, 64), 0.1)  # faint sky
scene[20, 22], scene[35, 40], scene[44, 18] = 30.0, 50.0, 20.0  # three point sources
y, x = np.indices((9, 9)) - 4
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
psfs = np.empty((9, 9, 1, 3))
images = np.empty((1, 64, 64, 3))
for k, sigma in enumerate((0.8, 1.0, 1.2)):
    psf = np.exp(-(x**2 + y**2) / (2 * sigma**2))
    psfs[:, :, 0, k] = psf / psf.sum()
    images[0, :, :, k] = convolve2d(scene, psfs[:, :, 0, k], mode="same") + rng.normal(0, 0.01, scene.shape)
print(images.shape, psfs.shape)

(1, 64, 64, 3) (9, 9, 1, 3)
The frame index is the last axis of both arrays.

text:
11.2 Save and validate a bundle
A bundle is a set of named arrays in one NPY directory, HDF5 file or Zarr store. Three arrays are required:








Key
Axes
Holds




images
(batch, y, x, frame)
the registered frames


variances
(batch, y, x, frame)
the variance of every pixel, finite and positive


psfs
(psf_y, psf_x, channel, frame)
one PSF per frame, square, odd-sized, one channel



An NPY bundle is a directory with one <key>.npy file per array. validate_bundle checks the array layout, mask dtype and exposure times and returns a list of issues. An empty list does not check every pixel value; check that the image and variance values are usable before reconstruction. summarize_bundle returns each array’s shape, dtype and axes.

from pathlib import Path
from cuphoton.ximage import load_ximage_bundle, summarize_bundle, validate_bundle

bundle_dir = Path("sample/ximage")
bundle_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
np.save(bundle_dir / "images.npy", images)
np.save(bundle_dir / "variances.npy", np.full_like(images, 0.01**2))
np.save(bundle_dir / "psfs.npy", psfs)

with load_ximage_bundle(bundle_dir) as bundle:
    print("issues:", validate_bundle(bundle))
    for key, info in summarize_bundle(bundle).items():
        print(f"{key:9s} {info['shape']} {info['axes']}")

issues: []
images    [1, 64, 64, 3] ['batch', 'y', 'x', 'frame']
variances [1, 64, 64, 3] ['batch', 'y', 'x', 'frame']
psfs      [9, 9, 1, 3] ['psf_y', 'psf_x', 'channel', 'frame']


Optional arrays use the same naming. masks is a boolean array shaped like images, True for a good pixel. exp_times holds one positive value per frame. xImage divides each frame by its exposure time and each variance by its square. The data contract lists every array.

text:
11.3 Write a configuration
A workflow reads its settings from a YAML file. xImage validates the file strictly. A misspelled key is an error. The repository has annotated examples in examples/ximage/. Copy the L2 example, point it at the bundle, and give the run a name that later runs can overwrite:

import os
import yaml

REPO = Path(os.environ.get("CUPHOTON_REPO", "."))
config = yaml.safe_load((REPO / "examples/ximage/reconstruct-l2.example.yaml").read_text())
config["data"]["base"] = "sample/ximage"
config["output"] = {"root_dir": "sample/runs", "name": "l2", "overwrite": True}
Path("sample/reconstruct-l2.yaml").write_text(yaml.safe_dump(config, sort_keys=False))
print(config["algorithm"], config["device"], config["dtype"], config["max_iter"], config["padding"], config["roi"])

l2 auto float64 75 VALID {'center': None, 'height': 48, 'width': 48}


The example reconstructs the central 48 by 48 pixels. With VALID padding, the frames must hold real pixels half a PSF beyond each edge of the region, 4 pixels for these 9 by 9 PSFs. device: auto runs on CUDA when PyTorch sees a GPU and on the CPU otherwise. Table 11.1 lists the keys you change first.

text:
11.4 Run the reconstruction
run_reconstruction takes the configuration’s path as a Path. It returns a WorkflowResult with the run directory and the summary, which the run also saves as its receipt.

from cuphoton.ximage.workflows import run_reconstruction

result = run_reconstruction(Path("sample/reconstruct-l2.yaml"))
summary = result.summary
print(result.run_dir.name, summary["backend"], summary["performance"]["device"]["device"], summary["dtype"])
print("saved image:", summary["image_shape"])
trace = summary["trace_summary"]
print(f"{trace['iterations_count']} iterations, loss {trace['loss_last']:.2f}, u_score {trace['u_score_last']:.1e}")

l2 torch cpu float64
saved image: [1, 56, 56, 1]
75 iterations, loss 2.97, u_score 7.9e-06


The saved image is the 48-pixel region plus the 4-pixel PSF border on each side. A run stops after max_iter iterations, or earlier once the update score u_score falls below stop_tol. The loss is the mean, over good pixels, of the squared residual divided by the variance.

11.5 Read the run directory
This reconstruction writes the following files:

print(sorted(str(p.relative_to(result.run_dir)) for p in result.run_dir.rglob("*") if p.is_file()))
image = np.load(summary["saved"]["image"])
scene_l2 = image[0, 4:-4, 4:-4, 0]  # drop the 4-pixel PSF border
print(image.shape, "->", scene_l2.shape)

['artifacts/image.npy', 'config.yaml', 'summary.json', 'trace/iterations.npy', 'trace/loss.npy', 'trace/u_score.npy']
(1, 56, 56, 1) -> (48, 48)


The files are the following:

config.yaml: the configuration as the run resolved it, with every default filled in.
summary.json: the receipt. It records the backend, device, dtype, cuPhoton version, input store, region, saved paths, a trace summary and timings.
artifacts/image.npy: the scene on the region plus its border.
trace/: the loss and update score at each iteration.

Crop the border before you use the scene, as the evaluation does. The scene is in exposure-time-normalized units. The run returns no output variance and no effective PSF for the scene. summary.json holds input paths and metadata. Review it before you share it.

text:
11.6 Evaluate the run
evaluate_reconstruction_run crops the scene to the region and compares it with a median coadd (the pixel-by-pixel median of the frames). It reports sharpness, sky scatter, PSNR and SSIM (two image-similarity scores), and the flux of detected sources.

from cuphoton.ximage.evaluation import evaluate_reconstruction_run

evaluation = evaluate_reconstruction_run(result.run_dir, metrics_backend="auto")
print(evaluation["metrics_backend"], evaluation["projection_shape"])
for name in ("restoration", "synthetic_coadd"):
    print(name, {key: round(value, 3) for key, value in evaluation[name].items() if isinstance(value, float)})
print("matched sources:", evaluation["photometry"]["matched_aperture_count"])

cpu [48, 48]
restoration {'sharpness_sf': 3.75, 'sky_sigma': 0.024, 'finite_pixel_fraction': 1.0}
synthetic_coadd {'sharpness_sf': 1.048, 'sky_sigma': 0.007, 'finite_pixel_fraction': 1.0, 'psnr_vs_restoration': 33.457, 'ssim_vs_restoration': 0.956}
matched sources: 3


restoration describes the scene and synthetic_coadd the median. Both come from the same frames and share their noise. Similarity or sharpness alone therefore does not show that a reconstruction is accurate.

text:
11.7 Calibrate the PSFs
With the frame PSFs, xImage aims for the scene itself, with point sources as single pixels. PSF calibration instead fits, for each frame, the kernel that blurs a narrow Gaussian of width sigma_g (0.55 pixels in the example) into that frame’s PSF. A reconstruction with these kernels returns the scene as seen through that Gaussian. run_psf_solve fits them with multiplicative updates (method: mm) or the Adam optimizer (method: adam).

from cuphoton.ximage.workflows import run_psf_solve

psf_config["data"]["base"] = "sample/ximage"
psf_config["output"] = {"root_dir": "sample/runs", "name": "psf-mm", "overwrite": True}
Path("sample/psf-mm.yaml").write_text(yaml.safe_dump(psf_config, sort_keys=False))
kernels = run_psf_solve(Path("sample/psf-mm.yaml"))
print(kernels.summary["method"], kernels.summary["psfs_shape"])
print(sorted(p.name for p in (kernels.run_dir / "artifacts").iterdir()))

12.1 Check the environment
xRay (cuphoton.xray) analyzes time-resolved X-ray detector data from pump-probe scans. A laser pulse excites the sample (the pump), and an X-ray pulse a set delay later records it on an area detector (the probe). Each delay gives one detector frame. You reduce a laser-on and laser-off pair of frame stacks to a trace and fit it as a sum of damped oscillations. On a GPU, the same fit runs on every detector row.
You need:
Run the xRay doctor on a new machine. It lists the libraries xRay found:

  cuPhoton: 0.3.0.dev98+gc04d1a5
  NumPy: 2.4.6
  CuPy: not installed

Capabilities:
  ok      numpy          [required] array operations
  ok      h5py           [required] HDF5 input
  missing cupy           [gpu] CUDA array kernels
  missing bokeh          [optional] interactive review views

Executables:
  missing nvidia-smi
  missing sbatch

CUDA visibility: empty
NumPy and h5py are required. The trace steps below run without CuPy; the GPU trace API and default detector-wide backend require it. Bokeh adds interactive review pages. Include this output in environment bug reports.
